patient.name: Winston Clarke
patient.complaint: Sudden severe pain in his left leg 2 hours ago; the foot is now white, cold and numb
background: Atrial fibrillation diagnosed last year; stopped his apixaban 2 months ago
Retired postman from Brixton, walks his dog daily without leg pain

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' with a sudden, cold, pale, pulseless leg in a patient with AF (acute limb ischaemia), against gradual claudication (chronic occlusion) or a pulsatile mass (aneurysm). The pain level tells you the site.

points: Winston, 74, felt **sudden severe pain** in his left calf while watching TV.
Within minutes the foot went **white and cold**.
No previous leg pain on walking.

steps.lead: Winston's problem is **acute** blockage, not dilation: the 'acute disease causes occlusion' half of the rule.

points: Left foot **pale** and **perishingly cold** to the knee.
Femoral pulse present; **popliteal and foot pulses absent**.
Reduced sensation over the foot; toe movement weak.

steps.lead: Winston has the **6 Ps**, including **paraesthesia** and early **paralysis**, so this limb is threatened.

steps.q: His femoral pulse is present but popliteal pulse absent. Where is the block?
steps.r: Pulse lost between the groin and the knee: **femoral-popliteal** occlusion, which gives pain **below the knee**.

steps.lead: Winston's calf pain and pulse loss below the groin put the block in the **femoral-popliteal** segment.

visual.title: Rhythm strip on arrival
visual.caption: Irregularly irregular, no P waves: **atrial fibrillation**, the commonest source of a limb embolus.

steps.lead: Winston's **AF**, untreated for 2 months, is the obvious source: a clot from the left atrium has **embolised** to his leg.
Winston's abdomen has a **pulsatile mass**: an **AAA** shares his risk factors. Rupture would mean sudden back pain and hypotension.

steps.text: A cold, pale, pulseless leg is **not** a DVT (warm, swollen, red). Sudden onset in a patient with chronic claudication is still **acute limb ischaemia**: acute on chronic.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?' (handheld Doppler at the bedside) or 'diagnostic investigation' (CT angiography). For chronic occlusion, ABPI; for AAA, ultrasound.

points: Handheld Doppler: **no signal** at dorsalis pedis or posterior tibial.
Bloods and group and save sent.

steps.lead: Winston's **handheld Doppler** at the bedside confirms no arterial flow below the knee within minutes.

steps.title: Winston's bloods
steps.text: Raised **lactate** and CK show muscle ischaemia. A normal INR confirms he is not anticoagulated.

visual.title: Winston's lactate
visual.label: Winston 3.6
visual.caption: Lactate reflects the **degree** of tissue ischaemia.

steps.q: Which imaging defines the site and extent of Winston's blockage?
steps.r: **CT angiography** is the gold standard: it shows exactly where the occlusion starts and how far it runs.

steps.lead: Winston's **CT angiogram** shows an abrupt cut-off in the distal superficial femoral artery with no collaterals (an embolus), and a small **AAA**.

steps.title: Investigating a vascular leg or abdomen
nodes: Acute limb: handheld Doppler at the bedside
Bloods: lactate, CK, U&E, clotting, group and save
steps.caption: Imaging must not delay treatment of a threatened limb.

steps.text: Chronic occlusion: **ABPI** is the first test. Below 0.9 suggests peripheral arterial disease; very low values mean critical ischaemia.
**Venous** duplex looks for DVT. A pale, pulseless leg needs **arterial** assessment: Doppler, then CT angiography.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial management?' (IV unfractionated heparin, analgesia, urgent vascular referral) and the definitive step (embolectomy within 6 hours). Long-term: antiplatelets, statin, lifestyle; aneurysms by size.

visual.title: Hours since Winston's symptoms began
visual.label: Winston 2.5 h
visual.caption: Muscle and nerve tolerate about **6 hours** of ischaemia.

steps.lead: Winston gets **oxygen, IV fluids and analgesia**, **IV unfractionated heparin**, and the vascular team takes him for **embolectomy** inside 6 hours.

steps.r: **IV unfractionated heparin** stops the clot propagating distally. It is easily reversed if he goes to theatre.

points: Embolectomy at 4 hours: a long clot is removed from the femoral artery.
Foot pulses return; the foot pinks up.

visual.title: After reperfusion
visual.caption: A brief rise as ischaemic muscle is **reperfused**, then recovery. Watch potassium and the calf compartments.

steps.lead: His CT angiogram also showed a **small 4.2 cm AAA**, so it goes on **surveillance**; smoking cessation, an antiplatelet or anticoagulant, and a **statin** cover his arterial disease.
Winston's acute care follows **Vascular Society** limb ischaemia guidance; his AAA and arterial disease follow **NICE**.

steps.text: After reperfusion, a tense, very painful calf with pain on passive stretch is **compartment syndrome**: it needs **fasciotomy**.
Embolic ALI from AF: after embolectomy, the long-term fix is **anticoagulation** (e.g. a DOAC) to stop the next embolus.

science.exam: Science questions ask why an embolus is so dramatic (no collaterals), why the 6-hour window exists (anaerobic tolerance) or why lactate rises.

steps.title: From AF to a dead limb
nodes: AF: stagnant blood in the left atrial appendage
Lodges at a narrowing or bifurcation

steps.lead: Winston's embolus hit a **normal** artery with no collateral network, so his leg went from fine to white in minutes.
Winston's rising lactate is **anaerobic metabolism**; after about **6 hours** muscle and nerve begin to die.

steps.r: Without oxygen, ischaemic muscle runs on **anaerobic glycolysis**, producing lactate.

steps.lead: Winston's smoking and hypertension gave him **both** an AAA (dilation) and arterial disease: same risk factors, different wall response.

steps.text: A patient who **already claudicates** has collaterals, so a thrombosis on their plaque often presents less dramatically than an embolus.

mcq.r: **Pain, perishingly cold, pulseless, pallor, paraesthesia, paralysis**.

mcq.r: **Handheld arterial Doppler**; ABPI and bloods are for chronic occlusion.

mcq.r: **IV UFH** prevents distal propagation of the thrombus.

Ruptured AAA: sudden abdominal/back pain and hypotension

prompts.tip: Exam thinking: bedside first, then the gold standard.

points.p: Handheld arterial Doppler at the bedside

prompts.tip: Exam thinking: ABPI for legs, ultrasound for aorta.

points.p: DR ABCDE: oxygen, IV fluids, analgesia

prompts.tip: Exam thinking: aneurysm by size; occlusion by risk factors.

points.p: Large aneurysm: EVAR or open repair

prompts.q: Why is embolic acute limb ischaemia so dramatic and time-critical?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: collaterals and anaerobic tolerance.

points.p: Sudden complete occlusion with no time for collaterals
points.why: Thrombosis on chronic disease has collaterals.

points.p: 6-hour window: limited anaerobic tolerance of muscle and nerve

prompts.tip: Exam thinking: one profile, two wall responses.

points.p: Shared risk factors: atherosclerosis, smoking, hypertension
Different wall response: dilation vs stenosis/occlusion
points.why: Chronic tends to aneurysm, acute to occlusion.

glossary.Acute limb ischaemia: Sudden loss of arterial blood supply to a limb, threatening its survival within hours.
glossary.6 Ps: Pain, pallor, pulseless, perishingly cold, paraesthesia and paralysis: the signs of acute limb ischaemia.
glossary.Paraesthesia: Pins and needles or numbness, here from ischaemic nerves.
glossary.Embolus: A clot or other material carried in the blood that blocks a distant artery.
glossary.Embolectomy: Surgical removal of an embolus, usually with a balloon catheter.
glossary.Paradoxical embolus: A venous clot that crosses to the arterial side through a hole in the heart, such as a PFO.
glossary.PFO: Patent foramen ovale: a small persistent opening between the atria.
glossary.Thrombosis: A clot forming in place, here on a narrowed atherosclerotic artery.
glossary.Collateral circulation: Alternative small vessels that bypass a gradually narrowing artery.
glossary.Intermittent claudication: Cramping leg pain on walking a predictable distance, relieved by rest.
glossary.PVD: Peripheral vascular disease: narrowing of the limb arteries by atherosclerosis.
glossary.PAD: Peripheral arterial disease, another name for PVD.
glossary.ABPI: Ankle-brachial pressure index: ankle over arm systolic pressure; below 0.9 suggests peripheral arterial disease.
glossary.Handheld Doppler: A bedside probe that turns arterial blood flow into sound.
glossary.CT angiography: CT scan with IV contrast that maps the arteries and shows blockages or aneurysms.
glossary.Unfractionated heparin: An IV anticoagulant that stops clots growing and can be quickly reversed.
glossary.Aneurysm: A permanent abnormal dilation of an artery.
glossary.EVAR: Endovascular aneurysm repair: a stent graft placed through the femoral arteries.
glossary.Atrial fibrillation: An irregularly irregular heart rhythm in which clots can form in the left atrium.
glossary.Lactate: A product of anaerobic metabolism; its level reflects how much tissue is ischaemic.
glossary.CK: Creatine kinase: a muscle enzyme released when muscle is damaged.
glossary.Reperfusion: Restoring blood flow, which can release potassium and acid from damaged muscle.
glossary.Compartment syndrome: Raised pressure in a muscle compartment that cuts off its blood supply.
glossary.Fasciotomy: Cutting the fascia to relieve compartment syndrome.
glossary.Femoral-popliteal: The arterial segment from the femoral artery in the thigh to the popliteal artery behind the knee.
glossary.Aortoiliac: The lower aorta and the iliac arteries that it divides into.
glossary.Inguinal ligament: The ligament in the groin; the external iliac artery becomes the femoral artery beneath it.
glossary.Atherosclerosis: Build-up of fatty plaques in artery walls, causing narrowing.
glossary.Anaerobic metabolism: Energy production without oxygen, which makes lactate.
glossary.Statin: A cholesterol-lowering drug that stabilises atherosclerotic plaques.
glossary.Antiplatelet: A drug such as clopidogrel or aspirin that stops platelets clumping.
glossary.DOAC: Direct oral anticoagulant, such as apixaban, used to prevent clots in AF.

technique.stem: A 66 year old man has a 6 month history of cramping pain in his right calf that comes on after walking about 100 metres and goes away after a few minutes of rest. He smokes 20 cigarettes a day. His right foot is cool and the right foot pulses are absent. There is no swelling.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: A diagnosis question: acute or chronic arterial disease?

clues: goes away after a few minutes of rest
steps.x: Gradual, predictable, rest-relieved calf pain with absent pulses: **chronic occlusion**, femoral-popliteal level.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: DVT gives a warm, swollen calf with pulses present.
Spinal stenosis eases with bending forward or sitting, and pulses are normal.
Neuropathy gives constant burning in a stocking distribution.
Venous insufficiency gives oedema, varicose veins and skin changes.

steps.x: **B.** Rule: calf pain on walking, relieved by rest, absent pulses = claudication (pain below the knee = femoral-popliteal).

technique.stem: A 70 year old man who smokes is found to have a pulsatile, expansile mass in the epigastrium during a routine check. He has no abdominal or back pain. His pulse rate is 78 bpm and BP 146/88 mmHg.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?

steps.x: Initial investigation of a suspected stable aneurysm.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Abdominal ultrasound** first-line to measure the diameter.

elim: CTA is for planning repair, not first-line.
Erect CXR looks for free air.
MRI is not first-line.
Plain AXR may show calcification but cannot measure the aneurysm reliably.

steps.x: **E.** Rule: AAA = ultrasound first; chronic leg occlusion = ABPI; acute limb = Doppler then CTA.

technique.stem: A 77 year old woman with atrial fibrillation has a 3 hour history of a cold, pale, pulseless left leg with reduced sensation. She has been given analgesia and IV unfractionated heparin, and the vascular team has been called.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate definitive management?

steps.x: Definitive management in embolic acute limb ischaemia.
Embolic ALI from AF, inside the 6-hour window, limb threatened.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Amputation is for an unsalvageable limb, not one at 3 hours.
Stockings are for venous disease and harm ischaemic legs.
Clopidogrel is long-term for chronic disease.
Exercise is for claudication.

steps.x: **C.** Rule: heparin first, embolectomy within 6 hours.

technique.stem: A 69 year old man has acute limb ischaemia. His surgeon explains that the leg must be revascularised within about 6 hours or it may not be saved. His serum lactate is raised.
technique.q: Which best explains why there is a 6 hour window?
o: Limited anaerobic tolerance of muscle and nerve
Venous return fails before arterial supply

steps.x: Ischaemic tissue runs on anaerobic metabolism, shown by lactate.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Skeletal muscle and nerve tolerate anaerobic conditions only for ~6 hours before **irreversible necrosis**.

elim: Collaterals do not close at 6 hours.
Heparin keeps working; it does not set the window.
Thrombus does not calcify in hours.
The problem is arterial inflow, not venous return.

steps.x: **C.** Rule: 6 hours = limited anaerobic tolerance; lactate measures it.

practice.stem: A 72 year old woman has a 1 hour history of sudden severe pain in her right leg. The leg is pale and cold below the knee and she cannot feel her toes. Her pulse rate is 118 bpm and irregularly irregular, and BP 152/90 mmHg. The right foot pulses are absent. ECG (see item resources).

visual.title: Rhythm strip on arrival
visual.caption: Irregularly irregular, no P waves: **atrial fibrillation**, the commonest source of a limb embolus.

practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Sudden pain, pallor, coldness, pulselessness and paraesthesia in a patient in AF is embolic acute limb ischaemia. DVT gives a warm swollen leg.

steps.x: Diagnosis: acute or chronic, arterial or venous?

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Cellulitis gives a hot red leg with fever.
DVT gives a warm swollen leg with pulses present.
Claudication is gradual and relieved by rest.
Sciatica gives shooting pain with normal pulses.

steps.x: **A.** Sudden cold pulseless leg + AF = acute limb ischaemia.

practice.stem: A 61 year old man who smokes has an 8 month history of cramping pain in both buttocks and thighs when walking uphill. It settles within minutes of resting. He also reports erectile dysfunction. Both femoral pulses are weak.
practice.q: Which is the most likely site of arterial disease?
practice.e: Buttock and thigh claudication with weak femoral pulses (and erectile dysfunction) points to aortoiliac occlusion.

steps.x: A site question: pain level tells you the level of the block.
Bilateral buttock/thigh pain with weak femoral pulses: the block is **above** the femorals.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Common femoral disease causes pain below the inguinal ligament.
Deep femoral disease causes thigh pain only.
External iliac disease is unilateral, just above the inguinal ligament.
Femoral-popliteal disease causes calf pain below the knee.

practice.stem: A 74 year old man has sudden pain and numbness in his left calf and foot. The foot is pale and cold. His left femoral pulse is palpable but the popliteal, dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses are absent. His pulse rate is 104 bpm and BP 138/84 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely site of occlusion?
practice.e: A palpable femoral pulse with an absent popliteal pulse and pain below the knee places the occlusion in the femoral-popliteal segment.

steps.x: A site question: find where the pulses stop.

clues: popliteal, dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses are absent
steps.x: Pulse present at the groin, lost at the knee; pain below the knee.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Aortoiliac occlusion would remove the femoral pulse.
Common femoral occlusion would remove the femoral pulse.
Deep femoral occlusion gives thigh pain and leaves distal pulses.
External iliac occlusion would remove the femoral pulse.

practice.stem: A 68 year old woman has a 2 hour history of a sudden cold, painful right leg. She has never had leg pain on walking and her left leg pulses are normal. Her pulse rate is 126 bpm and irregularly irregular, and BP 140/86 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely cause?
practice.e: Sudden onset, no prior claudication, a normal other leg and an irregularly irregular pulse mean an embolus from AF.

steps.x: A cause question: embolus or thrombosis?

clues: never had leg pain on walking
steps.x: No background PVD, normal other leg, AF: **embolic**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Dissection gives tearing chest/back pain and pulse deficits.
Paradoxical embolism needs a venous clot and a PFO, not AF.
Popliteal entrapment occurs in young athletes.
Thrombosis usually follows a history of claudication.

practice.stem: A 34 year old woman develops a sudden cold, pale left foot with absent foot pulses. She returned from a long-haul flight 3 days ago and has a swollen, tender right calf. An echocardiogram shows a patent foramen ovale. Her heart rhythm is regular.
practice.q: Which is the most likely cause of her acute limb ischaemia?
practice.e: A DVT (swollen calf after a flight) crossing a patent foramen ovale into the arterial system is a paradoxical embolus.

steps.x: A cause question in a young patient.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Dissection gives tearing chest pain.
Atherosclerosis is unlikely at 34 without risk factors.
Her rhythm is regular, so not AF.
Vasculitis is gradual with systemic features.

practice.stem: A 79 year old man has had a cold, pale, pulseless right leg for 5 hours. His temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 98 bpm and BP 150/82 mmHg. The vascular surgeon wants to know whether the limb is immediately threatened.
practice.q: Which finding most indicates advanced, limb-threatening ischaemia?
practice.e: Paralysis (with sensory loss) reflects ischaemic nerve and muscle damage: the limb is immediately threatened and needs urgent revascularisation.

steps.x: A finding question: which P is most severe?

clues: whether the limb is immediately threatened
steps.x: All 6 Ps can occur; nerve and muscle failure come last.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Pulselessness is present in all acute limb ischaemia.
Coldness is early.
Pain is usually the first symptom.
Pallor is early.

practice.stem: A 75 year old woman has a 1 hour history of a cold, pale left foot with no palpable foot pulses. Her pulse rate is 110 bpm and irregular. She is in the emergency department.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial bedside investigation?
practice.e: In acute limb ischaemia, a handheld arterial Doppler at the bedside confirms absent flow. CT angiography follows to define the site and extent.

steps.x: Initial bedside test in acute limb ischaemia.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: ABPI is for chronic occlusion.
CTA is the gold standard but not a bedside test.
MRA is slow and not used acutely.
Venous duplex looks for DVT.

practice.stem: A 70 year old man has acute limb ischaemia of his right leg. A handheld Doppler shows no flow at the ankle. He has received IV unfractionated heparin and the vascular team plans revascularisation.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to define the site and extent of the occlusion?
practice.e: CT angiography is the gold-standard investigation for acute limb ischaemia and chronic occlusion, defining the site and extent of the blockage.

steps.x: The surgeon needs a map of the blockage.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: ABPI cannot show where the block is.
D-dimer is for venous thromboembolism.
Plain X-ray does not show arteries.
Venous duplex does not assess arteries.

practice.stem: A 73 year old man with atrial fibrillation has a 2 hour history of a cold, pale, pulseless left leg. His pulse rate is 116 bpm and BP 144/90 mmHg. He has been given oxygen, IV fluids and analgesia.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate immediate drug treatment?
practice.e: IV unfractionated heparin prevents distal propagation of the thrombus and can be reversed for surgery. Oral agents are for long-term prevention.

steps.x: Immediate drug in acute limb ischaemia.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Apixaban is for long-term AF anticoagulation.
Clopidogrel is for chronic arterial disease.
A prophylactic dose is too low.
Warfarin takes days to work.

steps.x: **A.** ALI = IV UFH, then embolectomy within 6 hours.

practice.stem: A 74 year old man has a CT angiogram for leg pain. It shows an incidental 4.0 cm abdominal aortic aneurysm. He has no abdominal or back pain. His pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 138/80 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate management of the aneurysm?
practice.e: Aneurysms are managed by size: a small asymptomatic AAA is monitored with ultrasound surveillance; large ones are repaired by EVAR or open surgery.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Emergency repair is for rupture.
Repair is for large, symptomatic or rapidly growing aneurysms.
An aneurysm of 4.0 cm needs follow-up.
Laparotomy is for rupture or other emergencies.

steps.x: **D.** Small = surveillance; large = EVAR or open.

practice.stem: A 64 year old man has a 4 month history of left calf pain after walking 200 metres, relieved by rest. He smokes. His ankle-brachial pressure index is 0.7 on the left. There is no rest pain or tissue loss.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
practice.e: Chronic occlusion with claudication is managed first with lifestyle change, an antiplatelet and a statin. Revascularisation is for failure or critical ischaemia.

clues: no rest pain or tissue loss

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Bypass is for severe or limb-threatening disease.
IV heparin is for acute ischaemia.
Warfarin is not used for claudication.
Embolectomy is for acute embolic occlusion.

practice.stem: A 71 year old woman in atrial fibrillation develops a white, pulseless leg within minutes. Her husband, who has long-standing claudication, had a thrombotic occlusion of the same artery last year that caused only a mild worsening of his symptoms.
practice.q: Which best explains why her presentation is more severe?
practice.e: An embolus causes sudden complete occlusion with no time for collaterals to develop, whereas chronic atherosclerosis has already formed collaterals.

steps.x: A mechanism question comparing embolus with thrombosis.
Embolus in a normal artery vs thrombosis on chronic disease.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **No collateral circulation** in the embolic case.

elim: Viscosity is not the key difference.
Vessel size does not explain severity here.
Vasoconstriction is not the main mechanism.
This is arterial, not venous, disease.
